new_statements.rule_in_words: Portman's default for all five languages (Juwoi included) is stress on the first syllable of the word; any other stress position is lexically marked by underlining in his vocabulary. In the Juwoi column of the Comparative Vocabulary roots are almost always unmarked (hence initial), while the predicative suffix -lekíle regularly carries an underline on kí and a few roots are marked non-initially (Rá-chelúkāū 'centipede'). Juwoi-specific: a short vowel immediately before a stressed vowel is strongly reduced, and word-initial (prefixal) vowels often vanish (P'ling, K'lok, Y'róngap vs Puchikwar Pílang, Kúla, Yórangab), consistent with Zamponi & Comrie's (2021: 22) family-wide analysis 'non-phonemic stress.. falls on the initial syllable of the root'. Temple (1903: 115) restates it family-wide as 'Stress in Andamanese is placed on every long vowel, or on the first syllable of the root or stem'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said. (Portman's underlines on the suffix -lekíle alongside unmarked roots could be read as a second prominence on the predicative suffix, but he does not discuss it.)
new_statements.exceptions: Non-initial stresses are marked ad hoc by underline in the vocabulary (e.g. Juwoi Rá-chelúkāū p.27; suffix -lekíle passim). Temple 1903:116 adds for Juwai 'penultimate e is lengthened to é, and stressed é is drawled to éa'. Zamponi & Comrie 2021:22 hedge the family-wide root-initial rule with 'at least ordinarily'.
new_statements.domain_note: Portman's p.29 sentence is a reading convention for his transcriptions (word domain, citation forms in a comparative vocabulary), not an analytic claim; the p.30 Juwoi note describes pretonic reduction in connected/citation forms. Zamponi & Comrie's domain is the root (stress root-initial, prefixes unstressed), which fits the Juwoi apostrophe forms where the lost vowel is prefixal. Stress is stated to be non-phonemic family-wide (Z&C 2021). Language extinct; no instrumental or modern first-hand data possible.
new_statements.identity_note: Portman 1898 writes 'Āūkāū-Júwōī' and Temple 1903 'Juwai'; Radcliffe-Brown 1922 'Oko-Juwoi'; Glottolog/ISO 'Okojuwoi' [okj]. All refer to the same Middle Andaman tribe/language (okoj1239). Portman's stress convention (p.29) is stated once for all five 'South Andaman group' languages he records (Aka-Bea, Akar-Bale, Puchikwar, Aukau-Juwoi, Kol); the p.30 paragraph is specific to Aukau-Juwoi. Zamponi & Comrie 2021's statement is family-wide (Great Andamanese incl. Okojuwoi by name, p.9), made in a grammar of Akajeru (akaj1239).

sources.note: p.115: 'Peculiarities of Speech.—Stress in Andamanese is placed on every long vowel, or on the first syllable of the root or stem.' (family-wide, explicitly 'as described by Portman'; the long-vowel clause descends from the Ellis/Man 1882-85 Aka-Bea reading rule). p.116 JUWAI: 'Short vowels are not clearly marked.. Vanishing short vowels are common and are shown thus, j'rōngap : o is often drawled to ô : penultimate e is lengthened to é, and stressed é is drawled to éa.' Second-hand digest of Portman.
